title: Movement: Into, Through, Across and More
summary: Use common prepositions to describe where movement starts, which way it goes and the route it follows. Distinguish going inside, crossing, passing, climbing and moving around places.
learningObjectives: Use to, from, into and out of to describe destinations and movement into or out of spaces.
Describe movement onto or away from surfaces with on and off.
Use up, down, over and under to explain vertical movement and routes.
Distinguish through, round or around, along, across and past when describing a route.

explanation.heading: To, from, into and out of
explanation.body: To names a destination and from names a starting point: from the station to the park. Use into when someone or something moves from outside to inside a place; use out of when it leaves that space. In normally describes a position, and put something in a bag is usually more natural than put something into a bag.
explanation.example: A little bird flew into our kitchen through the open door.

explanation.heading: On and off
explanation.body: On can describe movement to a surface or onto certain forms of transport; off describes movement away from a surface. With public transport, we often say get on the bus and get off the bus. Take something off a shelf means remove it from the shelf.
explanation.example: My scarf fell off the chair and onto the floor.

explanation.heading: Up, down, over and under
explanation.body: Use up for movement towards a higher point and down for movement towards a lower one. Over describes crossing something from above, such as a low fence. Under describes a path below another object, such as going under a bridge.
explanation.example: The runners went up the steep path to the viewpoint.

explanation.heading: Through and round or around
explanation.body: Through describes passing into and across the inside of an opening, tunnel or area. Round (also around) describes following a curved path or going to the other side of something. A route can go through a park or around its edge: these are different paths.
explanation.example: We walked through a long tunnel beneath the town.

explanation.heading: Along, across and past
explanation.body: Along follows the length of a road, wall or river. Across goes from one side to the other. Past means going beyond a place or person on your way somewhere else. These words help make simple directions clear.
explanation.example: Go along the lane and then walk past the post office.

left.label: Into: movement
left.example: The child ran into the room.
left.note: The child moved from outside to inside the room.

right.label: In: position
right.example: The child is in the room.
right.note: The child is already inside the room.

left.label: Across: one side to the other

right.label: Along: following a line
right.example: We walked along the edge of the field.
right.note: Our route followed its edge rather than crossing it.

examples.sentence: The guests came out of the hall after the concert.
examples.note: Out of marks movement from inside to outside.

examples.sentence: The cyclist rode down the hill carefully.
examples.note: Down marks movement towards a lower place.

examples.sentence: A small boat passed under the wooden bridge.
examples.note: Under describes movement beneath an object.

examples.sentence: The children ran around the playground.
examples.note: Around can describe moving in a curved or circular route.

examples.sentence: We took a short path across the garden.
examples.note: Across describes a route from one side to another.

commonMistakes.incorrect: A rabbit jumped into of the box.
commonMistakes.correct: A rabbit jumped into the box.
commonMistakes.why: Into is one preposition; do not add of.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The cyclist rode up to the hill to reach the top.
commonMistakes.correct: The cyclist rode up the hill to reach the top.
commonMistakes.why: Up the hill describes movement along the slope; up to the hill means reaching the hill.

commonMistakes.incorrect: A child ran out the classroom.
commonMistakes.correct: A child ran out of the classroom.
commonMistakes.why: Out of is the normal phrase for leaving an enclosed space.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We walked past of the theatre.
commonMistakes.why: Past takes the place name directly, without of.

studyTips: Imagine drawing an arrow: into ends inside, out of starts inside, and across reaches the other side.
For directions, remember along the road, past the shop, through the tunnel and around the corner.
Compare get on a bus with get off a bus; compare go up a hill with go down a hill.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The puppy ran ___ the kitchen when we opened the door.
exercises.feedback: Into shows the puppy moved from outside the kitchen to inside it.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct expression: Maya took a clean cup ___ the cupboard and carried it to the sink.
exercises.feedback: Out of indicates that Maya removed the cup from inside the cupboard.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: We cycled ___ the hill, from the valley to the top.
exercises.feedback: Up shows movement from a lower point to a higher point.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: We swam ___ the river, from one bank to the other.
exercises.feedback: Across describes travelling from one bank to the opposite bank.

exercises.prompt: Complete with one word: We walked ___ the cinema without stopping; the café was further down the road.
acceptedAnswers: past
by
exercises.feedback: Past means going beyond a place; by is also natural in this sentence.

exercises.prompt: Complete with one word: We walked ___ the shore, following the coastline for an hour.
acceptedAnswers: along
exercises.feedback: Along describes following the length of the shore.

exercises.prompt: Complete with one word: The ball rolled ___ the stairs, from the top step to the bottom.
acceptedAnswers: down
exercises.feedback: Down expresses movement from the top to the bottom.

exercises.prompt: Complete with one word: The athlete jumped ___ the low wall and landed on the other side.
acceptedAnswers: over
exercises.feedback: Over describes crossing an obstacle above it.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The kitten jumped into of the empty box.
acceptedAnswers: The kitten jumped into the empty box.
exercises.feedback: Into already means movement inside, so of is unnecessary.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Smoke came out at the open window.
acceptedAnswers: Smoke came out of the open window.
exercises.feedback: Use out of, not at, to describe smoke leaving through the window.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The book fell off from the top shelf.
acceptedAnswers: The book fell off the top shelf.
exercises.feedback: Off is sufficient to show movement away from the shelf.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We walked past of the bakery on our way home.
acceptedAnswers: We walked past the bakery on our way home.
exercises.feedback: Past takes the noun phrase directly; do not add of.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the complete sentence using from and to: 'We walked ___ the station ___ the café.'
acceptedAnswers: We walked from the station to the café.
speakingExercises.feedback: From is the starting point; to is the destination.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the complete sentence using off: 'The notebook fell ___ the desk and landed on the floor.'
acceptedAnswers: The notebook fell off the desk and landed on the floor.
speakingExercises.feedback: Off indicates that the notebook left the desk’s surface.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the complete sentence using through: 'We drove ___ the tunnel before sunset.'
acceptedAnswers: We drove through the tunnel before sunset.
speakingExercises.feedback: Through describes travelling inside the tunnel from one end towards the other.

speakingExercises.prompt: A kitten runs from the hall to the inside of a cupboard. Describe its movement in one sentence. Begin 'The kitten ran', and include from the hall and into the cupboard.
acceptedAnswers: The kitten ran from the hall into the cupboard.
speakingExercises.feedback: From gives the starting point; into shows movement from outside to inside the cupboard.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change the direction in this sentence from uphill to downhill. Keep every other word the same: 'The hikers walked up the hill.'
acceptedAnswers: The hikers walked down the hill.
speakingExercises.feedback: Down shows movement towards a lower place; up would mean towards a higher place.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend needs to walk from one side of a narrow bridge to the other. Give one short instruction beginning 'Walk' and using across the bridge.
acceptedAnswers: Walk across the bridge.
speakingExercises.feedback: Across describes a route from one side of the bridge to the other.

speakingExercises.prompt: Someone says: 'We walked along the football field from one side to the other.' Correct only the direction word to match a route crossing the field. Say the complete corrected sentence.
acceptedAnswers: We walked across the football field from one side to the other.
speakingExercises.feedback: Across means crossing from one side to another; along means following the length of something.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give two short walking directions. First follow Hill Road lengthwise. Then pass the bakery without stopping. Begin the first instruction with 'Walk along' and the second with 'Then walk past'.
acceptedAnswers: Walk along Hill Road. Then walk past the bakery.
Walk along Hill Road, then walk past the bakery.
speakingExercises.feedback: Along describes following the road; past means continuing beyond the bakery.

listeningExercises.audioText: Lina stepped off the bus at the next stop.
listeningExercises.feedback: Stepped off the bus means Lina left the bus.

listeningExercises.audioText: The cyclist went around the park instead of riding through it.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which route did the cyclist take?
listeningExercises.feedback: The cyclist went around the park, not through it.

listeningExercises.audioText: We walked under the bridge to reach the riverside.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the movement word you hear immediately after “walked”.
acceptedAnswers: under
listeningExercises.feedback: Under describes the route below the bridge.

listeningExercises.audioText: The little rabbit ran into the shed and disappeared from view.
listeningExercises.feedback: Into indicates movement from outside to inside the shed.

listeningExercises.audioText: Follow the path along the river for two minutes, then cross the wooden bridge.
listeningExercises.prompt: What should the walker do first?
listeningExercises.feedback: First the walker follows the river; crossing the bridge is the next step.

listeningExercises.audioText: The cyclist rode over the bridge while a boat travelled under it.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which traveller took the lower route?
listeningExercises.feedback: The boat passed beneath the bridge, while the cyclist crossed on top of it.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children climbed up the steps to the old tower.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the one direction word you hear directly after 'climbed'.
acceptedAnswers: up
listeningExercises.feedback: Up shows movement towards a higher position on the steps.

listeningExercises.audioText: Emma hurried out of the classroom when the bell rang.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word movement expression you hear directly after 'hurried'.
acceptedAnswers: out of
listeningExercises.feedback: Out of describes movement from inside a room to outside it.
